subproblem.title: Differentiation under the integral sign: d/dt ∫ g(t⁻¹y) dμ(y) = −t⁻¹·∫ Dg(t⁻¹y)(t⁻¹y) dμ(y)
subproblem.statement: Let μ be a Borel measure on ℝ^N that is finite on compact sets and let g : ℝ^N → ℝ be a C¹ function with compact support, Dg = fderiv ℝ g. Then for every t > 0 the function r ↦ ∫ g(r⁻¹y) dμ(y) on ℝ (with the convention 0⁻¹ = 0, as in Lean; only its values near t matter) is differentiable at t with derivative −(t⁻¹·∫ Dg(t⁻¹y)(t⁻¹y) dμ(y)).
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (N : ℕ) (μ : Measure (Euclidean N)), IsFiniteMeasureOnCompacts μ → ∀ g : Euclidean N → ℝ, ContDiff ℝ 1 g → HasCompactSupport g → ∀ t : ℝ, 0 < t → HasDerivAt (fun r : ℝ => ∫ y, g (r⁻¹ • y) ∂μ) (-(t⁻¹ * ∫ y, fderiv ℝ g (t⁻¹ • y) (t⁻¹ • y) ∂μ)) t
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: steps 0, 1, 4 and 5 of the parent proof (pointwise t-derivative and differentiation under the integral sign), with all constants explicit.
Hypotheses: μ is a measure on ℝ^N = Euclidean N (Borel σ-algebra) with μ(K) < ∞ for every compact K (IsFiniteMeasureOnCompacts μ); g : ℝ^N → ℝ is C¹ with compact support; Dg := fderiv ℝ g. Fix t > 0. We prove that r ↦ ∫ g(r⁻¹y) dμ(y) has derivative −(t⁻¹·∫ Dg(t⁻¹y)(t⁻¹y) dμ(y)) at t.
1. (Integrability principle.) Every continuous f : ℝ^N → ℝ with compact support is μ-integrable (Continuous.integrable_of_hasCompactSupport, using IsFiniteMeasureOnCompacts μ).
2. (Constants.) tsupport g is compact, hence bounded: choose R₀ with tsupport g ⊆ B_{R₀}(0) (closed ball) and put R := max(R₀, 1), so R ≥ 1 > 0 and tsupport g ⊆ B_R(0). Since g is C¹, g is differentiable everywhere and Dg is continuous (ContDiff.differentiable, ContDiff.continuous_fderiv). Dg vanishes outside tsupport g (fderiv_of_notMem_tsupport), so Dg has compact support (HasCompactSupport.fderiv) and, being continuous, is bounded (Continuous.bounded_above_of_compact_support): choose L with ‖Dg(y)‖ ≤ L for all y; then L ≥ ‖Dg(0)‖ ≥ 0.
3. (Pointwise r-derivative.) Fix y ∈ ℝ^N and r > 0. The map ρ ↦ ρ⁻¹ has derivative −(r²)⁻¹ at ρ = r (hasDerivAt_inv, r ≠ 0), so ρ ↦ ρ⁻¹·y has derivative (−(r²)⁻¹)·y at ρ = r (HasDerivAt.smul_const). As g is differentiable at r⁻¹y, the chain rule (HasFDerivAt.comp_hasDerivAt) shows that ρ ↦ g(ρ⁻¹y) has derivative Dg(r⁻¹y)((−(r²)⁻¹)·y) at ρ = r. By linearity of Dg(r⁻¹y), Dg(r⁻¹y)((−(r²)⁻¹)·y) = −(r²)⁻¹·Dg(r⁻¹y)(y) = −(r⁻¹·(r⁻¹·Dg(r⁻¹y)(y))) = −(r⁻¹·Dg(r⁻¹y)(r⁻¹y)). Writing Φ(r,y) := −(r⁻¹·Dg(r⁻¹y)(r⁻¹y)), we conclude: for every y and every r > 0, ρ ↦ g(ρ⁻¹y) has derivative Φ(r,y) at ρ = r.
4. (Neighbourhood and dominating function.) Let I := (t/2, 2t). Since t/2 < t < 2t, I is an open interval containing t, hence a neighbourhood of t (Ioo_mem_nhds), and every r ∈ I satisfies r > t/2 > 0. Define b(y) := 2LR/t if ‖y‖ ≤ 2tR and b(y) := 0 otherwise, i.e. b is the indicator of the closed ball B_{2tR}(0) times the constant 2LR/t; b ≥ 0 because L ≥ 0, R > 0 and t > 0.
5. (Domination.) Let y ∈ ℝ^N and r ∈ I; we show |Φ(r,y)| ≤ b(y). Case r⁻¹y ∉ tsupport g: then Dg(r⁻¹y) = 0 (fderiv_of_notMem_tsupport), so Φ(r,y) = 0 ≤ b(y). Case r⁻¹y ∈ tsupport g: then ‖r⁻¹y‖ ≤ R; since y = r·(r⁻¹y) and r > 0, ‖y‖ = r·‖r⁻¹y‖ ≤ r·R ≤ 2t·R (as r < 2t and R > 0), so y ∈ B_{2tR}(0) and b(y) = 2LR/t. Moreover |Dg(r⁻¹y)(r⁻¹y)| ≤ ‖Dg(r⁻¹y)‖·‖r⁻¹y‖ ≤ L·R (operator-norm bound, using L ≥ 0), and 0 < r⁻¹ ≤ (t/2)⁻¹ = 2/t because r ≥ t/2 > 0 (inv_anti₀). Therefore |Φ(r,y)| = r⁻¹·|Dg(r⁻¹y)(r⁻¹y)| ≤ (2/t)·(L·R) = 2LR/t = b(y).
6. (Integrability and measurability.) (a) b is μ-integrable: the closed ball B_{2tR}(0) is measurable and compact, hence of finite μ-measure, so the constant 2LR/t is integrable on it (integrableOn_const) and its indicator b is integrable (integrable_indicator_iff). (b) For every r ∈ ℝ (with 0⁻¹ = 0), y ↦ g(r⁻¹y) is continuous (composition of g with the continuous map y ↦ r⁻¹y), hence a.e. strongly measurable. (c) y ↦ g(t⁻¹y) is continuous with compact support (HasCompactSupport.comp_smul, t⁻¹ ≠ 0), hence μ-integrable by step 1. (d) y ↦ Φ(t,y) = −(t⁻¹·Dg(t⁻¹y)(t⁻¹y)) is continuous (Dg is continuous; Continuous.clm_apply), hence a.e. strongly measurable.
7. (Dominated differentiation.) Apply Mathlib's hasDerivAt_integral_of_dominated_loc_of_deriv_le (Analysis/Calculus/ParametricIntegral.lean:286) with F(r,y) := g(r⁻¹y), F'(r,y) := Φ(r,y), base point t, neighbourhood I and bound b. Its hypotheses are: step 6(b) (F(r,·) is a.e. strongly measurable for r near t), step 6(c) (F(t,·) is integrable), step 6(d) (F'(t,·) is a.e. strongly measurable), step 5 (for every y and every r ∈ I, ‖F'(r,y)‖ ≤ b(y)), step 6(a) (b is integrable), and step 3 (for every y and every r ∈ I, ρ ↦ F(ρ,y) has derivative F'(r,y) at ρ = r, valid since r > 0). It yields that r ↦ ∫ g(r⁻¹y) dμ(y) has derivative ∫ Φ(t,y) dμ(y) at t.
8. (Rewriting the derivative.) ∫ Φ(t,y) dμ(y) = ∫ −(t⁻¹·Dg(t⁻¹y)(t⁻¹y)) dμ(y) = −∫ t⁻¹·Dg(t⁻¹y)(t⁻¹y) dμ(y) = −(t⁻¹·∫ Dg(t⁻¹y)(t⁻¹y) dμ(y)), by integral_neg and integral_const_mul (both valid without integrability hypotheses). Hence r ↦ ∫ g(r⁻¹y) dμ(y) has derivative −(t⁻¹·∫ Dg(t⁻¹y)(t⁻¹y) dμ(y)) at t. ∎
proof_key_steps: Fix R > 0 with tsupport g ⊆ B_R(0) and L ≥ 0 with ‖Dg‖ ≤ L (Dg continuous with compact support).
For y fixed and r > 0, ρ ↦ g(ρ⁻¹y) has derivative Φ(r,y) = −(r⁻¹·Dg(r⁻¹y)(r⁻¹y)) at ρ = r (hasDerivAt_inv, smul_const, chain rule, linearity).
On I = (t/2, 2t), |Φ(r,y)| ≤ b(y) := (2LR/t)·1_{B_{2tR}(0)}(y), which is μ-integrable (compact ball, finite measure).
hasDerivAt_integral_of_dominated_loc_of_deriv_le gives derivative ∫ Φ(t,y) dμ at t; integral_neg and integral_const_mul rewrite it as −(t⁻¹·∫ Dg(t⁻¹y)(t⁻¹y) dμ).

audit.reason: The prose and Lean type agree, including the total inverse convention. The pointwise derivative and its sign are correct. Compact support supplies R and a global derivative bound L; on (t/2,2t), the stated closed-ball indicator dominates the derivative uniformly and is integrable. Every measurability, integrability and neighbourhood hypothesis of the pinned dominated-differentiation theorem is supplied. Integral linearity gives exactly the stated derivative. The proof is complete and independent of the Euler identity and other children.

subproblem.title: Euler's identity applied to the dilates g(t⁻¹·): n·∫ g(t⁻¹y) dμ + ∫ Dg(t⁻¹y)(t⁻¹y) dμ = 0
subproblem.statement: Let μ be a Borel measure on ℝ^N that is finite on compact sets and let n ∈ ℕ. Suppose that ∫ (n·h(y) + Dh(y)(y)) dμ(y) = 0 for every C¹ function h : ℝ^N → ℝ with compact support (Dh = fderiv ℝ h). Then for every C¹ function g : ℝ^N → ℝ with compact support and every t > 0, n·∫ g(t⁻¹y) dμ(y) + ∫ Dg(t⁻¹y)(t⁻¹y) dμ(y) = 0, where Dg = fderiv ℝ g.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (N n : ℕ) (μ : Measure (Euclidean N)), IsFiniteMeasureOnCompacts μ → (∀ g : Euclidean N → ℝ, ContDiff ℝ 1 g → HasCompactSupport g → ∫ y, ((n : ℝ) * g y + fderiv ℝ g y y) ∂μ = 0) → ∀ g : Euclidean N → ℝ, ContDiff ℝ 1 g → HasCompactSupport g → ∀ t : ℝ, 0 < t → (n : ℝ) * (∫ y, g (t⁻¹ • y) ∂μ) + ∫ y, fderiv ℝ g (t⁻¹ • y) (t⁻¹ • y) ∂μ = 0
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: steps 0, 2 and 3 of the parent proof (the hypothesis (H) applied to the dilates g(t⁻¹·)).
Hypotheses: μ is a measure on ℝ^N = Euclidean N (Borel σ-algebra) with μ(K) < ∞ for every compact K (IsFiniteMeasureOnCompacts μ), n ∈ ℕ, and
 (H) ∫ (n·h(y) + Dh(y)(y)) dμ(y) = 0 for every C¹ function h : ℝ^N → ℝ with compact support, where Dh(y) := fderiv ℝ h y.
Fix a C¹ function g : ℝ^N → ℝ with compact support and t > 0; write c := t⁻¹ (so c ≠ 0) and Dg := fderiv ℝ g. We prove n·∫ g(c·y) dμ(y) + ∫ Dg(c·y)(c·y) dμ(y) = 0.
1. (Integrability principle.) Every continuous f : ℝ^N → ℝ with compact support is μ-integrable: it is bounded and vanishes outside the compact set tsupport f, which has finite μ-measure (Continuous.integrable_of_hasCompactSupport, using IsFiniteMeasureOnCompacts μ).
2. (The dilate is C¹ with compact support.) Let g_c(y) := g(c·y). The map y ↦ c·y is a continuous linear map, hence C^∞ (contDiff_id.const_smul c), so g_c = g ∘ (y ↦ c·y) is C¹ (ContDiff.comp). Its support is c⁻¹·(support g); since y ↦ c·y is a homeomorphism of ℝ^N (c ≠ 0), tsupport g_c is the image of the compact set tsupport g under y ↦ c⁻¹·y, hence compact (HasCompactSupport.comp_smul with c ≠ 0).
3. (Derivative of the dilate.) g is C¹, hence differentiable at every point (ContDiff.differentiable, as 1 ≠ 0). The map y ↦ c·y has derivative c·id at every y (hasFDerivAt_id together with HasFDerivAt.const_smul). By the chain rule (HasFDerivAt.comp), Dg_c(y) = Dg(c·y) ∘ (c·id), so for every y, Dg_c(y)(y) = Dg(c·y)(c·y).
4. (The two summands are integrable.) (a) y ↦ n·g(c·y) is a constant multiple of the continuous compactly supported function g_c (step 2), hence integrable (step 1; Integrable.const_mul). (b) Let k(y) := Dg(c·y)(c·y). Dg is continuous because g is C¹ (ContDiff.continuous_fderiv), y ↦ c·y is continuous, and the value of a continuous linear map at a vector depends continuously on both (Continuous.clm_apply), so k is continuous. The function x ↦ Dg(x)(x) vanishes at every x ∉ tsupport g, because g ≡ 0 on a neighbourhood of such an x and so Dg(x) = 0 (fderiv_of_notMem_tsupport); hence its support lies in the compact set tsupport g and it has compact support (HasCompactSupport.mono'). k is that function composed with y ↦ c·y, so k has compact support (HasCompactSupport.comp_smul, c ≠ 0). By step 1, k is integrable.
5. (Apply (H) and split the integral.) By step 2, (H) applies to h = g_c and gives ∫ (n·g(c·y) + Dg_c(y)(y)) dμ(y) = 0. Rewriting the integrand pointwise with step 3 gives ∫ (n·g(c·y) + Dg(c·y)(c·y)) dμ(y) = 0. By step 4 both summands are integrable, so the integral of the sum is the sum of the integrals (integral_add), and ∫ n·g(c·y) dμ(y) = n·∫ g(c·y) dμ(y) (integral_const_mul). Therefore n·∫ g(t⁻¹y) dμ(y) + ∫ Dg(t⁻¹y)(t⁻¹y) dμ(y) = 0. ∎
proof_key_steps: The dilate g_t(y) = g(t⁻¹y) is C¹ (composition with the linear map y ↦ t⁻¹y) with compact support (HasCompactSupport.comp_smul).
Chain rule: Dg_t(y)(y) = Dg(t⁻¹y)(t⁻¹y) for every y.
y ↦ n·g(t⁻¹y) and y ↦ Dg(t⁻¹y)(t⁻¹y) are continuous with compact support (Dg vanishes off tsupport g), hence μ-integrable.
Apply the hypothesis to g_t, rewrite the integrand, and split with integral_add and integral_const_mul.

audit.reason: All hypotheses and the conclusion match the Lean type. Positive t makes dilation a linear homeomorphism, preserving C¹ regularity and compact support. The chain-rule identity is correct. Continuity and the derivative's vanishing outside tsupport g establish integrability of both summands before integral_add is used. subproblem.title: A solution of F′(t) = n·F(t)/t on (0,∞) satisfies F(s) = sⁿ·F(1)
subproblem.statement: Let n ∈ ℕ and let F : ℝ → ℝ be a function such that, for every t > 0, F is differentiable at t with derivative F′(t) = n·F(t)/t. Then F(s) = s^n·F(1) for every s > 0.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (n : ℕ) (F : ℝ → ℝ), (∀ t : ℝ, 0 < t → HasDerivAt F ((n : ℝ) * F t / t) t) → ∀ s : ℝ, 0 < s → F s = s ^ n * F 1
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: step 7 of the parent proof (integration of the ODE), isolated as a statement about an arbitrary real function F.
Hypotheses: n ∈ ℕ, F : ℝ → ℝ, and for every t > 0, F has derivative n·F(t)/t at t (HasDerivAt F (n·F(t)/t) t). Fix s > 0; we prove F(s) = s^n·F(1).
1. (The auxiliary function.) Define G : ℝ → ℝ by G(r) := F(r)/r^n (with the convention x/0 = 0, as in Lean; only the values of G on (0,∞) are used).
2. (Derivative of G.) Fix t > 0. Then t ≠ 0 and t^n ≠ 0 (pow_ne_zero). The map r ↦ r^n has derivative n·t^(n−1) at t (hasDerivAt_pow; here n − 1 is truncated subtraction in ℕ, which only matters when n = 0). By hypothesis F has derivative n·F(t)/t at t. By the quotient rule (HasDerivAt.fun_div, applicable because t^n ≠ 0), G has derivative
 G'(t) = ((n·F(t)/t)·t^n − F(t)·(n·t^(n−1))) / (t^n)²
at t.
3. (G'(t) = 0.) Case n = 0: the real number n equals 0, so both products in the numerator are 0, the numerator is 0, and G'(t) = 0/(t^0)² = 0. Case n = m + 1: then n − 1 = m and t^(m+1) = t^m·t, so (n·F(t)/t)·t^(m+1) = n·F(t)·t^m·(t/t) = n·F(t)·t^m because t ≠ 0, and this equals F(t)·(n·t^m); hence the numerator is 0 and G'(t) = 0. Thus G has derivative 0 at every t > 0.
4. (G is constant on (0,∞).) The set (0,∞) = Ioi 0 is open (isOpen_Ioi) and preconnected (isPreconnected_Ioi). By step 3, G is differentiable at every point of (0,∞), hence differentiable on (0,∞), and deriv G t = 0 for every t ∈ (0,∞). By the zero-derivative theorem on an open preconnected set (IsOpen.is_const_of_deriv_eq_zero), G takes equal values at any two points of (0,∞); as s ∈ (0,∞) and 1 ∈ (0,∞), G(s) = G(1).
5. (Conclusion.) G(1) = F(1)/1^n = F(1), so F(s)/s^n = F(1). Since s > 0, s^n ≠ 0, so F(s) = F(1)·s^n = s^n·F(1) (div_eq_iff, commutativity of multiplication). ∎
proof_key_steps: For t > 0, G(t) := F(t)/t^n has derivative ((n·F(t)/t)·t^n − F(t)·n·t^(n−1))/(t^n)² at t (hasDerivAt_pow and the quotient rule HasDerivAt.fun_div, t^n ≠ 0).
The numerator vanishes: trivially if n = 0; if n = m+1 because (n·F(t)/t)·t^(m+1) = n·F(t)·t^m. So G has derivative 0 at every t > 0.
(0,∞) is open and preconnected, so IsOpen.is_const_of_deriv_eq_zero gives G(s) = G(1) = F(1) for s > 0.
Multiply F(s)/s^n = F(1) by s^n ≠ 0 to get F(s) = s^n·F(1).

audit.reason: The one-line Lean proposition exactly matches the prose. The quotient rule applies because t^n is nonzero; the numerator cancellation correctly handles n=0 separately. Differentiability and zero derivative on the open preconnected positive half-line justify constancy, and evaluation at 1 proves the conclusion. The proof is complete, independent and non-circular.
